comp.label: The Triangle
comp.compStory:
In the school orchestra, Ravi played the triangle. He had not chosen it. Nobody chooses the triangle. It had been handed to him in Year Four by Mrs Pell, the music teacher, along with a small metal beater and the words, "Every orchestra needs one," which Ravi had since come to suspect was the sort of thing adults said about jobs nobody wanted.

The triangle has, at most, a handful of notes in any piece. In the spring concert piece, a long and rather stormy work called "Harbour Lights", Ravi had exactly four. He spent the remaining nine minutes counting. He counted bars the way other people counted sheep, except that if he fell asleep, everyone would know.

"You're lucky," said Maddie, who played first violin and had notes in every single bar. "You can't play a wrong note."

"I can play a right note at the wrong time," said Ravi. "That's worse. Everyone hears it."

Maddie considered this and, to her credit, did not laugh.

Three days before the concert, Mrs Pell lost her voice. It went on Monday morning with a sound like a door creaking shut, and by lunchtime she could manage only a whisper and a great many hand signals. On Tuesday she did not come in at all. On Wednesday, the day of the dress rehearsal, the head teacher appeared in the music room looking as though she had been asked to land an aeroplane.

"Mrs Pell is very sorry," she said. "She's hoping to be back tomorrow for the concert. In the meantime, she asks that one of you leads the rehearsal." She looked down at a note in her hand, clearly written in a hurry. "She says: Ravi."

Thirty heads turned. Ravi felt his face grow hot, as if someone had opened an oven door in front of it.

"Me? I play the triangle."

The head teacher checked the note again. "She says, and I quote, 'Ravi has counted every bar of this piece. He knows where everyone comes in.'"

It was true. That was the strange part. In nine minutes of counting, Ravi had done nothing else but listen. He knew that the cellos always came in a fraction late after the quiet section, because they were waiting for the flutes, who were waiting for them. He knew that the brass played too loudly in the storm, so that the violins had to scrape to be heard. He knew exactly where the music fell apart, because he had spent months sitting inside the moment just before it did.

He stood up. His legs did not feel entirely like his own.

The first run-through was a disaster. He waved his arms; nobody watched them. The cellos were late. The brass were deafening. When it ended, there was a long and painful silence, broken only by a trumpet player sniggering into his sleeve.

Ravi looked at the floor. Then, because there was nothing else to do, he looked at the cellos.

"You're waiting for the flutes after the quiet bit," he said. "Don't. Come in on my hand." He turned to the flutes. "And you're waiting for them. So nobody goes. Watch me instead." He turned, more bravely now, to the brass. "In the storm, you're drowning everyone else. It's supposed to sound like the wind. Not like a lorry."

Someone laughed, but it was a different kind of laugh this time.

The second run-through was better. The third was good. By the fourth, the cellos came in exactly on his hand, and the storm sounded like weather rather than traffic, and the violins rose over the top of it, clear and bright. When the last chord faded, the room was quiet in a way that felt nothing like the silence before.

"Ravi," said Maddie slowly. "You've missed all your triangle notes."

He had. Every one.

Mrs Pell's voice returned on Thursday, just about. She conducted the concert in a scarf, whispering instructions that only the front row could hear, but it hardly mattered: everyone knew the piece now. Ravi stood at the back with his small metal beater and played his four notes, each one exactly on time.

Afterwards, Mrs Pell found him packing away.

"Every orchestra needs one," she croaked, and nodded at the triangle.

This time, Ravi thought he understood what she meant. It had never really been about the triangle at all. It was about having somebody who was listening to everyone else.

questions.subject: ENGLISH
questions.quest: What did Ravi suspect about the words "Every orchestra needs one"?
questions.optionA: That Mrs Pell wanted him to give up music
questions.optionB: That the orchestra was short of players
questions.optionC: That the triangle was the hardest instrument
questions.optionD: That adults say it to make an unpopular job sound important
questions.explanation: He thought it was 'the sort of thing adults said about jobs nobody wanted'.

questions.subject: ENGLISH
questions.quest: How many notes did Ravi have to play in "Harbour Lights"?
questions.explanation: 'In the spring concert piece... Ravi had exactly four.'

questions.subject: ENGLISH
questions.quest: "He counted bars the way other people counted sheep, except that if he fell asleep, everyone would know." What does this sentence suggest?
questions.optionA: Ravi often fell asleep during concerts
questions.optionB: Counting was dull, but he had to stay alert because a mistake would be obvious
questions.optionC: Ravi found counting exciting and relaxing
questions.optionD: Ravi could not count very well
questions.optionE: The orchestra was playing a piece about sheep
questions.explanation: Counting sheep is boring and sends you to sleep; unlike that, Ravi could not afford to drift off.

questions.subject: ENGLISH
questions.quest: Why does Ravi say playing "a right note at the wrong time" is worse than a wrong note?
questions.optionA: Because the triangle only has one note
questions.optionB: Because wrong notes are not allowed in concerts
questions.optionC: Because Mrs Pell would be angry
questions.optionD: Because Maddie would laugh at him
questions.optionE: Because a triangle note stands out, so a badly timed one is heard by everyone
questions.explanation: 'Everyone hears it': with so few notes, any mistake in timing is very noticeable.

questions.subject: ENGLISH
questions.quest: Mrs Pell's voice went "with a sound like a door creaking shut". What does this simile suggest?
questions.optionB: Her voice faded away slowly and croakily until it stopped
questions.optionC: She had hurt her throat on a door
questions.optionD: Her voice suddenly became very high
questions.optionE: She slammed the door of the music room
questions.explanation: A creaking door closes slowly with a rough sound, like her voice failing.

questions.subject: ENGLISH
questions.quest: The head teacher looked "as though she had been asked to land an aeroplane". What does this suggest?
questions.optionA: She felt out of her depth in charge of the orchestra
questions.optionB: She had recently been on an aeroplane
questions.optionC: She wanted to leave the school
questions.optionD: She was excited about the concert
questions.optionE: She was annoyed with Mrs Pell
questions.explanation: Landing a plane is a task most people could not do; she feels unqualified and anxious.

questions.subject: ENGLISH
questions.quest: Why did Mrs Pell choose Ravi to lead the rehearsal?
questions.optionA: He had asked to be the conductor
questions.optionB: He was the oldest member of the orchestra
questions.optionC: He had the fewest notes to play
questions.optionE: He had counted every bar and knew where everyone came in
questions.explanation: The note says he 'has counted every bar of this piece. He knows where everyone comes in.'

questions.subject: ENGLISH
questions.quest: "That was the strange part." What did Ravi find strange?
questions.optionA: That by playing so little he had come to know the whole piece extremely well
questions.optionC: That the head teacher knew his name
questions.optionD: That the triangle was in the concert at all
questions.optionE: That Mrs Pell had written him a note
questions.explanation: His boring job of counting had made him listen to everything, which gave him an unexpected skill.

questions.subject: ENGLISH
questions.quest: Why did the cellos and the flutes both come in late?
questions.optionA: Each group was waiting for the other to start first
questions.optionB: The brass were playing too loudly
questions.optionD: Their music was missing some pages
questions.optionE: They could not see Mrs Pell
questions.explanation: The cellos 'were waiting for the flutes, who were waiting for them'.

questions.subject: ENGLISH
questions.quest: "His legs did not feel entirely like his own." What does this show about Ravi?
questions.optionB: He was so nervous that his body felt strange and unsteady
questions.optionC: He was wearing someone else's trousers
questions.optionE: He had been sitting down for too long
questions.explanation: Nerves make his legs feel shaky, as if they belonged to someone else.

questions.subject: ENGLISH
questions.quest: Why did Ravi look at the cellos after the first run-through?
questions.optionA: He was waiting for the cellos to apologise
questions.optionB: He wanted to see who was laughing
questions.optionC: He decided to tackle the problems he had noticed, one group at a time
questions.optionD: He was too embarrassed to look at the brass
questions.optionE: He had forgotten what to do
questions.explanation: 'Because there was nothing else to do', he starts using what he knows, beginning with the late cellos.

questions.subject: ENGLISH
questions.quest: "It's supposed to sound like the wind. Not like a lorry." What is Ravi telling the brass players?
questions.optionC: They are playing the wrong piece
questions.optionE: They are playing far too heavily and loudly for the music
questions.explanation: Wind is a sweeping sound; a lorry is heavy and noisy, so they are overpowering the others.

questions.subject: ENGLISH
questions.quest: "Someone laughed, but it was a different kind of laugh this time." How had the laugh changed?
questions.optionA: It was friendly and approving, not mocking
questions.optionE: It was meant to upset Ravi
questions.explanation: The first was a snigger at Ravi; this one shows the orchestra enjoying his joke and accepting him.

questions.subject: ENGLISH
questions.quest: How does the writer show the rehearsals improving?
questions.optionA: By describing what Ravi ate for lunch
questions.optionB: By listing the names of all the players
questions.optionC: By describing each run-through as better than the last, ending with the music sounding right
questions.optionD: By showing the head teacher conducting
questions.optionE: By having Mrs Pell return during the rehearsal
questions.explanation: 'The second run-through was better. The third was good. By the fourth...' builds steady improvement.

questions.subject: ENGLISH
questions.quest: Maddie says, "You've missed all your triangle notes." What does this show?
questions.optionB: Ravi did not want to play the triangle any more
questions.optionC: Ravi had been so busy leading that he forgot his own part
questions.optionD: The triangle had been left at home
questions.explanation: Conducting took all his attention, a gently funny twist after his worries about timing.

questions.subject: ENGLISH
questions.quest: Mrs Pell "croaked" her words after the concert. What does "croaked" tell us?
questions.optionC: She spoke in a rough, hoarse voice
questions.optionD: She spoke in a cheerful voice
questions.explanation: Her voice had only 'just about' returned, so it was hoarse.

questions.subject: ENGLISH
questions.quest: Which word best describes how Ravi changes during the story?
questions.optionA: From unsure of his worth to confident in his skill
questions.explanation: He begins thinking his role is pointless and ends understanding the value of listening.

questions.subject: ENGLISH
questions.quest: What is the main message of the story?
questions.optionA: Teachers should never lose their voices
questions.optionB: The triangle is the most important instrument
questions.optionC: A role that seems small can matter a great deal, especially if you pay attention
questions.optionD: Concerts are always a disaster without practice
questions.optionE: Only the loudest players are important
questions.explanation: Ravi's 'unwanted' job made him the one person who was 'listening to everyone else'.

questions.subject: MATHS
questions.quest: What is 59 × 46?

questions.subject: MATHS
questions.quest: What is 7/12 + 5/8?

questions.subject: MATHS
questions.quest: A club has 96 members and 5/8 of them are girls. How many girls are there?

questions.subject: MATHS
questions.quest: A bike costs £120. Its price goes up by 15%. What is the new price?

questions.subject: MATHS
questions.quest: Orange squash is mixed with water in the ratio 3 : 5. How much squash is needed to make 400 ml of drink?
questions.explanation: There are 8 parts, so one part is 50 ml. Squash is 3 parts: 150 ml.

questions.subject: MATHS
questions.quest: Solve 6x + 5 = 2x + 33.
questions.explanation: Subtract 2x: 4x + 5 = 33, so 4x = 28 and x = 7.

questions.subject: MATHS
questions.quest: The sequence 50, 44, 38, 32, … continues. What is the 12th term?
questions.explanation: It goes down by 6 each time. The 12th term is 50 − 11 × 6 = −16.

questions.subject: MATHS
questions.quest: The mean of six test scores is 16. Five of the scores are 14, 18, 11, 18 and 20. What is the sixth score?
questions.explanation: Six scores with mean 16 total 96. 14 + 18 + 11 + 18 + 20 = 81, so the sixth is 96 − 81 = 15.

questions.quest: Find the angle marked y in this quadrilateral.

questions.subject: MATHS
questions.quest: A rectangular lawn is 12 m by 8 m. A rectangular flower bed 4 m by 3 m is cut out of it. What area of lawn is left?

questions.subject: MATHS
questions.quest: A cube has edges of 5 cm. What is its volume?

questions.subject: MATHS
questions.quest: A shop opens at 09:50 and closes at 14:35. How long is it open?
questions.explanation: 09:50 to 13:50 is 4 hours; 13:50 to 14:35 is 45 minutes.

questions.subject: MATHS
questions.quest: What is the highest common factor of 36 and 48?
questions.explanation: Factors of 36 include 12 and 18; factors of 48 include 12 and 16. The largest number in both lists is 12.

questions.subject: MATHS
questions.quest: Which of these is the same as 9/20?

questions.subject: MATHS
questions.quest: What is 7.465 rounded to 1 decimal place?
questions.explanation: The hundredths digit is 6, so round the tenths up: 7.465 → 7.5.

questions.subject: MATHS
questions.quest: A spinner has 15 equal sections and 6 of them are green. What is the probability of NOT landing on green?
questions.explanation: 15 − 6 = 9 sections are not green: 9/15 = 3/5.

questions.subject: MATHS
questions.quest: Three children have 62 stickers altogether. Jay has 6 more than Kim, and Lou has twice as many as Kim. How many does Kim have?
questions.explanation: Kim k, Jay k + 6, Lou 2k: 4k + 6 = 62, so 4k = 56 and k = 14.

questions.subject: MATHS
questions.quest: Ben buys 3 drinks at £2.40 each and 2 sandwiches at £1.85 each. He pays with a £20 note. How much change does he get?

questions.subject: MATHS
questions.quest: A train travels at 120 km/h for 1 hour 30 minutes. How far does it go?

questions.subject: VERBAL
questions.quest: In a code, BEAD is written as AFBC. How would TOAST be written in the same code?
questions.explanation: Vowels move forward one letter and consonants move back one: T→S, O→P, A→B, S→R, T→S.

questions.subject: VERBAL
questions.quest: In a code, LION is written as OPJM. How would BEAR be written in the same code?
questions.explanation: The word is written backwards and then each letter moves forward one: BEAR → RAEB → SBFC.

questions.subject: VERBAL
questions.quest: Find the next letter: A, B, E, J, Q, ?
questions.explanation: The gaps are 1, 3, 5, 7, so the next gap is 9: Q → Z.

questions.subject: VERBAL
questions.quest: Find the next number: 1, 3, 4, 7, 11, 18, ?
questions.explanation: Each number is the sum of the two before it: 11 + 18 = 29.

questions.subject: VERBAL
questions.quest: Find the next number: 3, 6, 4, 8, 6, 12, ?
questions.explanation: The steps take turns: × 2, then − 2. 12 − 2 = 10.

questions.subject: VERBAL
questions.quest:
The numbers in each group are related in the same way. Find the missing number.
5 (22) 3     4 (9) 7     6 ( ? ) 10
questions.explanation: Square the first number and take away the second: 25 − 3 = 22, 16 − 7 = 9, 36 − 10 = 26.

questions.subject: VERBAL
questions.quest:
Which letter ends the first word and starts the second word in BOTH pairs?
pea ( ? ) ite        dar ( ? ) ing
questions.explanation: peak, kite and dark, king. R makes pear and rite, but not a word ending dar-r.

questions.subject: VERBAL
questions.quest:
Three letters that make a word have been taken out of the word in capitals. Which three letters complete it?
The TAIN steered the ship safely into the harbour.
questions.explanation: CAP + TAIN = CAPTAIN.

questions.subject: VERBAL
questions.quest: Which word can go in front of all of these to make three new words?  ___ball   ___fall   ___flake
questions.explanation: snowball, snowfall, snowflake. Rain, foot, water and night each fail with at least one.

questions.subject: VERBAL
questions.quest: Which word is most nearly the OPPOSITE of RELUCTANT?
questions.explanation: Reluctant means unwilling; the opposite is eager.

questions.subject: VERBAL
questions.quest: Which word is closest in meaning to METICULOUS?
questions.explanation: Meticulous means paying great attention to detail: thorough.

questions.subject: VERBAL
questions.quest: Which word belongs with: oak, ash, elm?
questions.explanation: Oak, ash and elm are trees; so is birch. An acorn and a leaf are parts of a tree.

questions.subject: VERBAL
questions.quest: Ali, Bea and Cy each have one pet: a dog, a cat or a fish. Ali is allergic to fur. Bea's pet does not live in water. Cy does not have a cat. Who has the dog?
questions.explanation: Ali cannot have fur, so Ali has the fish. Cy has no cat, so Cy has the dog and Bea has the cat.

questions.subject: VERBAL
questions.quest: The 3rd of a month is a Monday. What day of the week is the 26th of the same month?
questions.explanation: The 26th is 23 days after the 3rd. 23 = 3 weeks + 2 days, so it is two days after Monday: Wednesday.

questions.subject: VERBAL
questions.quest:
Rearrange the letters in capitals to make a word that completes the sentence sensibly.
The cat curled up by the fire and fell PALSEE.
questions.explanation: PALSEE can make ASLEEP or PLEASE, but only 'fell asleep' makes sense.

questions.subject: VERBAL
questions.quest: Which word can NOT be made using only the letters of TEMPERATURE? (Each letter may be used only as many times as it appears.)
questions.explanation: TEMPERATURE has no O, so PARROT cannot be made.

questions.subject: VERBAL
questions.quest: Bird is to flock as wolf is to ?
questions.explanation: A group of birds is a flock; a group of wolves is a pack.

questions.subject: VERBAL
questions.quest:
Change one letter at a time to turn PINE into LANE. Which word could go in the middle?
PINE → ? → LANE
questions.explanation: PINE → LINE (P to L) → LANE (I to A). The others need more than one change at a step.

questions.subject: VERBAL
questions.quest:
Find the number that completes the third pair in the same way as the first two.
(6 → 35)   (9 → 80)   (4 → ?)
questions.explanation: Square the number and take away 1: 36 − 1 = 35, 81 − 1 = 80, 16 − 1 = 15.

questions.subject: VERBAL
questions.quest: Ana, Ben, Cat and Dan sit around a square table, one on each side, facing the middle. Ana sits opposite Ben. Cat sits on Ana's left. Who sits on Ben's left?
questions.explanation: Facing the middle, Ana's left is Ben's right. Cat is on Ana's left, so Cat is on Ben's right, leaving Dan on Ben's left.
